title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Dog walking
audience: Dog walkers who want more work from businesses and property managers in their area, and who want to contact them lawfully.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide the walks you want before you look for them
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want. Write down the walk types you do well (solo walks, small groups, weekly routes), the price you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs a walk. A recurring weekly walk on a route you already run is worth far more to a small business than a single visit across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows.

instruction.heading: Score prospects against the criteria
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. Ask whether it sits inside your area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who makes the buying decision, and whether the walks fall within the permit and insurance you hold. Holiday rental managers and property managers with several sites inside your area are examples to evaluate, but add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Record the date each entry was added and where its contact details came from. Use only contact details published for business use. Do not buy or harvest lists: ACMA's guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (ACMA, 28 March 2019; an older source). Whether the Privacy Act applies depends on turnover and other factors, so check the OAIC's small business guidance.

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely in the near future. Examples include a public notice of planned building works, a new business opening on a route you already walk, a change of occupier at a site you already serve, or a competitor closing in your area. Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals. Do not monitor private people, use personal information that is not public, enter private property, or go to a home to make an offer. Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts (Victorian Government, 7 August 2026). Some councils publish a planning permit register, such as the City of Casey register on Victoria's open-data portal, so check your own council's register.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the business or the notice. It makes one specific observation that you can verify from public view or from the business's own published material. It then offers one small next step, such as a written price for a defined route or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026), so an honest message that names you is also a practical advantage.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. One reminder after a week and one final message after two further weeks, then a pause, is one pattern you can test. Stopping is part of the approach. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work.

procedure: Write the walk type, suburb, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and a contact source.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with its source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, and against your permit and insurance, before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, follow up on the fixed schedule, and remove anyone who asks you to stop.

workedExamples.situation: A dog walker covers three suburbs. A serviced-apartment block in one of them posts a public notice about planned courtyard works for the next two months, and its property manager's business email is published on the block's contact page. The walker's route passes the block, and she has no existing link to the manager.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should she send a sales message to the manager now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: She should not send a sales email just because the address is published. ACMA's guidance on the Spam Act says that publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages (ACMA, last updated 28 March 2019; an older source). She first checks whether the manager has agreed to receive marketing or has invited contact. If not, she waits for an invitation or uses a route the manager has agreed to. If she calls a registered number, she checks the Do Not Call Register first; the industry guide in the research gives telemarketing hours of weekdays 9am to 8pm and Saturdays 9am to 5pm, with no calls on Sundays or public holidays (2018 copyright notice, so check for updates). Any message names the notice, says how she learned of it, offers one specific item she could handle, and asks one question. She does not contact residents using private details, and she does not enter the courtyard without an invitation. She offers walks for guests' dogs only if her permit and insurance cover them.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, walk type and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a walk you are not permitted or insured to deliver
commonErrors.prevention: Check the permit and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a permitted service in outreach unless you hold the permit that the council where the walk happens requires. This lesson does not grant any permit, licence or authority. Permit rules differ between councils, so check the rule for each council you walk in.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Spam Act text was not read for this research, so check it before sending.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC guidance says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned
summary: Define the walks you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should a dog walker contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned works at a building on your route. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each resident using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the works
Go into the common area to look at the work before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
